name: AI Query Optimisation
title: AI Query Optimisation
answer: Query optimisers choose how a database executes a query, and AI query optimisation applies machine learning to parts of that job: estimating how many rows a step will return, recommending which indexes to build, and tuning configuration settings that shape the plan. The work sits between database engineering and applied machine learning, and it matters because a plan choice made by a model can be hard to explain when it goes wrong. A practitioner here is usually a database engineer or data platform lead rather than a machine learning specialist, and the goal is a plan that is fast and repeatable, not a model that is clever.

sections.body: Query optimisers choose how a database executes a query, and AI query optimisation applies machine learning to parts of that job: estimating how many rows a step will return, recommending which indexes to build, and tuning configuration settings that shape the plan. The work sits between database engineering and applied machine learning, and it matters because a plan choice made by a model can be hard to explain when it goes wrong. A practitioner here is usually a database engineer or data platform lead rather than a machine learning specialist, and the goal is a plan that is fast and repeatable, not a model that is clever.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs against the database engine itself and the statistics it keeps, so the first dependency is a query workload that can be captured and replayed. Teams collect query text, execution plans, runtimes and schema metadata into a store, then train and evaluate models on that history, often on the same hardware class as production so timings mean something. Cloud warehouses and managed database services expose plan and statistics data through their own interfaces, which shapes what can be collected. Nothing here replaces the optimiser, it feeds it better inputs or adjusts the settings around it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The common pattern is to treat plan quality as a prediction problem: learn from past executions what a query shape will cost, then use that estimate where the optimiser's own statistics are weak. Index advisors search candidate index sets against a workload and score them by estimated benefit, and configuration tuners adjust memory and parallelism settings against measured throughput. Evaluation is done by replaying a workload and comparing plans, runtimes and resource use, with care taken to hold out queries so the model is not scored on what it memorised. Because plans are discrete and feedback is delayed, teams often keep a rule based fallback and a way to pin a known good plan.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risk is opacity: when a learned estimate or a recommended index makes a query slower, the reason may not be visible in the plan, so teams need logging, versioning of models and statistics, and a rollback path. Changes to indexes or settings touch production data and cost, so they usually go through review and staged rollout rather than automatic application. Provenance matters too, since a model trained on one workload or schema version may not transfer, and that history should be recorded alongside the model. On medical, legal or financial data the usual access controls and retention rules apply to the workload data used for training, and none of this is a substitute for advice from the relevant specialist.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is tighter coupling between learned components and the optimiser, with learned cardinality estimates and index recommendations becoming ordinary features of managed database services rather than separate research projects. Expect more emphasis on explainability and on guardrails that bound how far a learned choice can deviate from a proven plan. Workloads will keep changing, so the practical question is less whether a model can beat the current optimiser on a benchmark and more whether it can be retrained, audited and reverted safely in a live system.
